name: Owain Glyndŵr
role: Welsh prince and leader of the revolt against English rule, 1400–c.1415
summary: Glyndŵr sought an independent hereditary Welsh principality, supported by foreign allies. His program combined ecclesiastical autonomy and universities with territorial ambitions beyond Wales.

sources.title: Pennal Letter and declaration, 1406, Appendix 1
sources.author: Owain Glyndŵr; Matthews 1910 translation reproduced by Cadw
sources.usedFor: Read full declaration, pages 59–62, and report’s historical discussion, pages 13–16.

sources.title: 1401 letters and Tripartite Indenture, reproduced in Owen Glyndwr (1901)
sources.author: Owain Glyndŵr and treaty partners; translated documents in A. G. Bradley
sources.usedFor: Downloaded book, searched themes; read full Scottish and Irish letters and indenture, separating documents from romanticized narration.

sources.title: Owain Glyndwr (1959)
sources.author: Thomas Jones Pierce, Dictionary of Welsh Biography
sources.usedFor: Read complete biography; Welsh independence, enlarged territorial claims and uncertain connections to social grievances.

sources.title: Tripartite Indenture
sources.author: Owain Glyndŵr Society
sources.usedFor: Boundary text and context for the proposed division of England and Wales.

sources.title: The Rise and Fall of Owain Glyn Dwr: review, 2017
sources.author: Richard Brown, Historical Association
sources.usedFor: Read review of Gideon Brough’s study, including revolt, native parliaments and French military aid.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Requested ancestral privileges for princely heirs.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Proposed restored archiepiscopal authority over dioceses.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Expressly included heirs as future princes.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Pledged enduring mutual military support with allied lords while preserving his French alliance.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Justified his claim through alleged descent from Britain’s ancient rulers.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Sought restoration of native Welsh princely leadership against rule by the Saxons he denounced.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.

more-religion-public.rationale: Integrated ecclesiastical reform into Welsh statehood.

national-church-status.rationale: Sought a privileged, independent Welsh church.

national-self-determination.rationale: Sought Welsh independence from English government; this documents Wales’s claim, not a universal theory.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Wanted restored Welsh ecclesiastical traditions and Welsh-speaking clergy.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Sought heresy penalties for church desecration.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Recognized Benedict alone for his subjects.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Invoked ancestral Welsh sovereignty when seeking military aid against English rule.

right-to-secede.rationale: Led armed separation of Wales from the English crown.

separate-church-state.rationale: Made papal obedience a public settlement.

territorial-expansion.rationale: His partition agreement claimed substantial English territory beyond conventional Welsh boundaries.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Presented the Welsh as continuing the people of Cadwallader and legendary Brutus.

notes: Pennal’s religious punishment request concerns church destruction, not a general apostasy law. Universities imply no tuition policy. Assemblies of notables establish no modern democratic franchise. Transmitted letters and treaty texts receive medium confidence where original-document provenance is indirect. Legendary ancestry is his claim, not accepted genealogy. Older biography’s dates and reconstructions yield to modern corroboration. Patronage, opposition to heavy taxation and proposed restoration of Welsh law do not specify an economic blueprint or every traditional family rule. No inference from lordship, military service, bardic praise or later nationalist folklore fills remaining nulls after review across all ten themes.
